findings.rationale: The file ends with asyncio.run(main(False)) at module scope (line ~130) rather than under an if __name__ == '__main__' guard, unlike the quickstart examples which do guard (quickstart_neo4j.py:241, quickstart_falkordb.py:252). Importing this module triggers clear_data(client.driver) and graph ingestion against the configured database.
findings.title: Module-level asyncio.run(main(False)) executes on import

findings.rationale: neo4j_password = os.environ.get('NEO4J_PASSWORD') or 'password' (line 36) supplies a literal default credential when the env var is unset, and the same pattern appears in examples/ecommerce/runner.py:36, examples/wizard_of_oz/runner.py:35, and examples/quickstart/quickstart_neo4j.py:51. These are example scripts, but the fallback silently connects with a well-known password.
findings.title: Example runner hardcodes default Neo4j password fallback

findings.rationale: sanitize() only translates a separator_map and collapses whitespace (lines 244-247), then build_fulltext_query concatenates the sanitized user query into a Cypher string: full_query = group_filter + ' (' + sanitized_query + ')' (line 278). The query text is interpolated into the query string rather than passed as a bound parameter, so the sanitize step is the only barrier. This is the parser/network_entry hotspot surface for the FalkorDB driver.
findings.title: FalkorDB fulltext query built by string concatenation after weak sanitize()

findings.rationale: group_values = '|'.join(group_ids) (line 264) is embedded into the group_filter portion of the fulltext query string, and the length check at line 275 uses len(group_ids or '') which is a length guard, not an escaping guard. group_ids flow from caller-supplied values (e.g. graphiti.py group_ids params) into a concatenated query.
findings.title: group_ids joined into query string without parameterization

findings.rationale: get_by_group_ids builds cursor_query as a LiteralString ('AND e.uuid < $uuid' if uuid_cursor ...) and concatenates it into the query, with group_ids passed as a bound parameter (group_ids=group_ids, line 215). The group_ids themselves are parameterized, but the cursor clause is string-concatenated; this is the high-complexity edge query path flagged in the hotspot.
findings.title: Edge.get_by_group_ids interpolates cursor clause into Cypher

findings.rationale: _extract_json_from_text finds the first '{' and last '}' and json.loads the slice (lines ~120-135). This is the parser-tagged hotspot: it will mis-parse when the model emits multiple JSON objects or braces inside strings, and it raises ValueError carrying the full model response text in the message.
findings.title: _extract_json_from_text uses brace-slicing to parse model output

findings.rationale: When config is None, the client constructs LLMConfig() and sets config.api_key = os.getenv('ANTHROPIC_API_KEY') (lines ~93-96). This is the auth_boundary/network_entry hotspot: the API key is read from the process environment and passed to AsyncAnthropic, so any code path that instantiates the client without an explicit config silently inherits ambient credentials.
findings.title: AnthropicClient falls back to ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var when config omitted

findings.rationale: _get_cache_key builds key_str = f'{self.model}:{message_str}' and returns hashlib.md5(key_str.encode()).hexdigest() (lines ~128-131). MD5 is used here for cache-key derivation, not for a security boundary, but it is the crypto-tagged hotspot in this file and collisions could cause cross-message cache reuse of LLM responses.
findings.title: LLM response cache key uses MD5 over model+messages

findings.rationale: generate_response appends the response_model JSON schema to messages[-1].content and appends MULTILINGUAL_EXTRACTION_RESPONSES to messages[0].content (lines ~150-160) before computing the cache key. Because the same list object is mutated, repeated calls accumulate appended instructions and change the cache key, which is a correctness/state-leak concern in the shared LLM client path.
findings.title: generate_response mutates caller-supplied messages list in place

findings.rationale: _check_safety_blocks collects safety_ratings category/probability into safety_info and raises Exception(f'Response blocked by Gemini safety filters: {safety_details}') (lines ~120-135). Raising a bare Exception (rather than a typed error) from the response-parsing path means callers cannot distinguish safety blocks from other failures, and the message embeds model-provided content.
findings.title: Safety-block handling raises bare Exception with response details

findings.rationale: In __init__, when no client is supplied, self.client = genai.Client(api_key=config.api_key) (line ~95). This is the auth_boundary/network_entry hotspot for the Gemini path; the API key is taken from LLMConfig and used to build the outbound client, with no validation that the key is present before the network client is created.
findings.title: GeminiClient constructs genai.Client with config.api_key

findings.rationale: In the KUZU and default branches, labels are interpolated via f-string into MATCH (n:{label} {{uuid: $uuid}}) (e.g. lines ~100 and ~130). The label values are hardcoded literals ('Episodic','Community','Entity'), so this is not currently attacker-controlled, but it is the high-complexity delete path flagged in the hotspot and the pattern is unsafe if labels ever become dynamic.
findings.title: Node.delete interpolates label into f-string Cypher

findings.rationale: The hotspot reports loc=1889 and nesting=35 for graphiti_core/search/search_utils.py, the largest and most deeply nested file in the set, tagged auth_boundary and network_entry with reachability=5. The grep for query construction shows this module is the search/query layer, so its depth makes the query-building paths hard to audit for parameterization.
findings.title: search_utils.py is a 1889-line module with nesting depth 35

findings.rationale: argparse registers parser.add_argument('--destroy-graph', action='store_true', help='Destroy all Graphiti graphs') (line 1192), and the module imports clear_data from graphiti_core.utils.maintenance.graph_data_operations (line 38). This is the network_entry/auth_boundary hotspot: a single CLI flag drives destructive deletion of all graphs with no confirmation or scoping shown in the argument definition.
findings.title: MCP server exposes --destroy-graph flag that clears all graphs

findings.rationale: GraphitiLLMConfig.from_cli_and_env(cls, args) (line 266) and GraphitiConfig.from_cli_and_env (line 492) build configuration by combining argparse Namespace values with environment variables, and the module imports DefaultAzureCredential/get_bearer_token_provider (line 15) and AsyncAzureOpenAI (line 17). This is the auth_boundary surface where CLI-supplied values and ambient cloud credentials converge into the LLM/embedder clients.
findings.title: GraphitiLLMConfig.from_cli_and_env merges CLI args with environment credentials
